analogy.p: Imagine asking for a journey. A high-level instruction is 'Take me to the airport': it is short and easy for a person to say, but the driver must work out every turn. Low-level instructions are 'turn left in 50 metres, then second exit at the roundabout, then 3 km straight': extremely precise and efficient for that exact route, but long, tiring to write and useless if you are in a different city. Machine code is like giving the car's engine every individual signal. The analogy breaks down because a computer cannot interpret vague instructions, so a translator must do the working-out that the driver does.
analogy.t: Giving directions in different levels of detail

bullets: **High-level language**: written using English-like keywords and structures (for example Python, Java, C#, Visual Basic); designed for humans to read, write and debug.
**Low-level language**: close to the hardware and the CPU's own instruction set; the two examples to know are **assembly language** and **machine code**.
The scale runs from machine code (closest to hardware) through assembly language to high-level languages (closest to human language).
**Abstraction** means hiding detail: a high-level programmer writes print() without worrying about registers, memory addresses or CPU instructions.
The CPU can only ever run machine code, so every program in any other language must be **translated** before it can run.
The choice of level is a trade-off between ease of development and control over the hardware; examiners reward answers that make this trade-off explicit.
core.h: What a programming language is and why there are different levels
core.p: A **programming language** is a set of rules and keywords used to write instructions (a program) that a computer can carry out. The only language a CPU can actually execute is **machine code**, which is made entirely of binary (1s and 0s). Because binary is extremely hard for humans to read and write, programming languages have been developed at different **levels of abstraction**: the further a language is from the hardware, the closer it is to human language. OCR J277 divides languages into **high-level** and **low-level**, and you must know the characteristics, purpose, advantages and disadvantages of each.

bullets: Uses English-like **keywords**, readable variable names and structures such as selection (if), iteration (for, while) and subprograms (functions and procedures).
**One statement = many machine code instructions** (a one-to-many relationship), so programs are shorter and faster to write.
**Portable**: not tied to one processor, so the same source code can be translated for different computers (a suitable translator is needed for each).
Easier to **read, understand, debug and maintain** by other programmers, which matters for large team projects.
Needs a **translator** (compiler or interpreter) to convert it into machine code before the CPU can execute it.
The programmer has little or no control over exactly which registers or memory locations are used, because the translator decides this.
Typical uses: desktop and mobile applications, websites, games, business software and most school programming.
core.p: High-level languages use words and symbols that resemble English and mathematics, so statements such as if, while, for and print are easy to recognise. One high-level statement usually represents **many** machine code instructions, so a programmer can express complex ideas in a few lines. The language hides hardware details, which means the same source code can normally be used on different types of computer. This makes programs quicker to write, easier to read and easier to maintain, at the cost of less direct control over the hardware.

bullets: Made of **binary only**; the CPU's control unit decodes each instruction during the fetch-decode-execute cycle.
**No translator is needed** because it is already in the form the processor can execute.
**Processor (machine) dependent**: code for one processor architecture (for example an Intel x86 CPU) will not run on another (for example an ARM CPU).
Extremely difficult to read, write, debug or modify; a single wrong bit changes the meaning of an instruction.
Gives the programmer **complete control** over the hardware, memory and registers.
Final output of every translator: whatever language a program is written in, it must end up as machine code to be executed.
Also called **object code** or the executable when it is the output of a compiler.
core.p: **Machine code** is the binary instruction set that the CPU understands directly, written as patterns of 1s and 0s. Each instruction is made up of an **opcode** (what to do) and usually an **operand** (the data or address to use). Machine code needs **no translation**, so it is the fastest form for the CPU to execute, but it is almost impossible for humans to write without making mistakes. Every family of processors has its own instruction set, so machine code written for one type of CPU will not run on a different type.

bullets: Uses **mnemonics** (for example LDA, ADD, SUB, STA, INP, OUT, HLT in the OCR Little Man Computer style) plus operands such as memory addresses or labels.
**One-to-one relationship**: one assembly instruction translates to one machine code instruction (unlike high-level languages).
Still **processor specific**, so assembly written for one CPU architecture will not work on another without rewriting.
Translated by an **assembler** (see the separate topic on translators).
Easier to read and write than machine code, but much harder than a high-level language, and programs are long because every small step must be written out.
Lets the programmer control exactly how memory and registers are used, which allows very efficient programs.
The programmer must understand the CPU's architecture, for example its registers and instruction set.
core.p: **Assembly language** is a low-level language that replaces the binary patterns of machine code with short, memorable text codes called **mnemonics**, such as LDA (load), ADD, STA (store) and HALT. Because it is easier for a person to remember ADD than a string of binary digits, assembly is simpler to write than machine code, but it is still tied closely to one type of processor. Assembly language is converted into machine code by a translator called an **assembler**. Each assembly instruction normally corresponds to exactly **one** machine code instruction.

bullets: **Embedded systems** (such as a washing machine controller or a car engine management unit) often have very little memory and processing power, so compact efficient code is needed.
**Device drivers** and operating system components must communicate directly with hardware.
**Real-time systems** (for example airbag controllers) need very predictable, fast execution.
Programs can be made to run **faster** and take **less memory** because the programmer chooses exactly which instructions are used.
Direct access to **registers and memory addresses** allows control that a high-level language does not offer.
Disadvantages in these cases are the long development time, difficulty of debugging, and lack of portability, which is acceptable when the hardware never changes.
core.p: Low-level languages are chosen when the programmer needs **direct control of the hardware** or when the program must be as small and fast as possible. Because there is no extra layer hiding the hardware, the code can be tuned to use the least memory and the fewest processor cycles. These properties are essential in small devices with very limited resources and in software that talks directly to hardware. You should be able to link the scenario in a question to these needs.

bullets: **Quicker and cheaper to develop**: fewer lines are needed and built-in functions and libraries save effort.
**Easier to debug and test** because the code is readable and error messages refer to the source lines.
**Portable**: the same program can be used on many types of computer by using the right translator.
**Easier to maintain and update**, which is important when software has a long life or many developers.
Can use **structured programming constructs** (selection, iteration, subprograms) that make programs well organised.
Disadvantages: translation is needed, programs can be less efficient in speed and memory, and the programmer cannot control the hardware directly.
core.p: Most software is written in high-level languages because the saving in programmer time and the reduction in mistakes usually outweigh any small loss of speed. Modern computers are fast and have plenty of memory, so the extra efficiency of hand-written low-level code is rarely needed for ordinary applications. High-level code is also easier to share between programmers and to update when requirements change. For these reasons it is the default choice unless there is a specific reason to use low-level code.

bullets: **Readability**: high-level is English-like and easy to read; low-level (especially machine code) is hard to read.
**Translation**: high-level needs a compiler or interpreter; assembly needs an assembler; machine code needs none.
**Portability**: high-level is portable between processors; low-level is specific to one processor type.
**Instructions**: one high-level statement becomes many machine code instructions; one assembly instruction becomes one machine code instruction.
**Speed and memory**: low-level code can be made faster and smaller because the programmer controls the hardware; high-level code is usually less efficient.
**Development**: high-level is faster to write, debug and maintain; low-level takes longer and needs expert knowledge.
**Hardware control**: low-level gives direct control of memory and registers; high-level hides them.
core.p: A comparison question expects you to name a feature and then say what is true for **each** type of language, rather than describing them separately. Useful features to compare are readability, how translated, portability, speed of execution, memory control, development time and error finding. Always make the comparison explicit using words such as 'whereas' or 'but'. Remember that machine code is the fastest and most efficient for the CPU but the least friendly for the programmer.

bullets: **Source code** is the program as written by the programmer in a high-level or assembly language.
**Machine code / object code** is the binary output that the processor can execute.
Assembler: assembly language to machine code.
Compiler: translates a whole high-level program into machine code in one go, producing an executable file.
Interpreter: translates and runs a high-level program one statement at a time.
Each translator's detailed characteristics are covered in the next topic (compilers, interpreters and assemblers).
core.h: Why translators are needed and how this links to levels
core.p: Because the CPU only understands machine code, any program not already in machine code must pass through a **translator**. Translators convert **source code** (what the programmer writes) into **object code** or machine code (what the CPU runs). The type of translator depends on the language being translated: assembly uses an **assembler**, while high-level languages use a **compiler** or an **interpreter**. The translator is therefore the bridge between the human-friendly language and the hardware.

bullets: Source code written in Python can run on Windows, macOS or Linux provided an appropriate interpreter is installed.

A compiled program (the .exe or other executable) is **not** portable: it is machine code for a specific processor and operating system, so it must be compiled again for each platform from the portable source code.
Assembly for an ARM processor (used in most phones) will not work on an Intel x86 processor (used in many PCs).
Portability reduces cost because developers do not need to rewrite the program for every device.
Machine code and assembly are chosen over portable code only when the target hardware is fixed, as in an embedded device.
core.p: A program is **portable** if it can be moved to a different type of computer and still work with little or no change. A high-level language is portable because the source code does not mention any particular CPU; a suitable compiler or interpreter on each computer turns it into that computer's own machine code. Low-level code names specific instructions and registers of one processor family, so it is not portable. This is a very common exam point and is worth explaining in a sentence rather than just stating 'portable'.

bullets: High-level examples: **Python, Java, C#, Visual Basic, JavaScript, PHP**.
Low-level examples: **assembly language** and **machine code** (the two named in the OCR specification).
Assembly example in LMC-style: LDA 90, ADD 91, STA 92 (load a number, add another, store the result).
Machine code example: a binary string such as an 8-bit opcode followed by an operand.
Use of low-level: firmware in a washing machine, a microwave or a car's engine control unit.
Use of high-level: a mobile game, a school database system, a website.
core.h: Examples to quote in the exam
core.p: Examiners like specific examples because they show that you recognise real languages. Quote them as supporting evidence, but do not rely on naming a language as an explanation by itself. Python, Java, C#, Visual Basic and JavaScript are high-level; assembly language and machine code are low-level. Be careful: C and C++ are often described as high-level languages that allow some low-level control, so they are best avoided as an example unless the question asks.

bullets: Step 1: identify the **key features of the scenario** (hardware, memory limits, team size, how often it changes, speed needed).
Step 2: give **advantages of the suggested language** linked to the scenario, not generic ones.
Step 3: give **disadvantages or limits** and, if appropriate, an advantage of the alternative.
Step 4: write a short **justified conclusion** ('Overall a low-level language is more suitable because...').
Use correct terms: translator, portable, mnemonic, one-to-many, hardware control, memory efficient.
Avoid vague words like 'better', 'easier' or 'faster' without saying why and for whom.
core.p: OCR often sets a scenario and asks which type of language is more suitable, using the command word **discuss**. A top-mark answer states benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of the scenario and finishes with a justified conclusion. Match each point to a feature of the scenario: limited memory points towards low-level; many programmers and frequent updates point towards high-level; a need to run on several devices points towards high-level. A one-sided answer cannot reach the top mark band.

bullets: **CPU architecture (Paper 1)**: instructions are fetched, decoded and executed in binary form, using the registers and the control unit.
**Embedded systems (Paper 1)**: low-level languages are often used because the hardware is fixed and limited.
**Translators (this section)**: compilers, interpreters and assemblers do the conversion between levels.
**IDEs (this section)**: provide editors, error diagnostics and built-in translators for high-level development.
**Binary and data representation**: explains why machine code is stored as binary patterns.
**Software development**: the language chosen affects testing, maintenance and portability of the final product.
core.p: Languages and levels connect to several other parts of the course. The CPU's fetch-decode-execute cycle only ever works on machine code, which is why every program is reduced to it. Assembly language links to the architecture topic through registers such as the accumulator and the program counter. The translator topic follows directly from this one, and data representation explains why machine code is binary. Making these links helps you write more complete explanations.

exam: **Describe** (2 marks): give two linked points, e.g. 'High-level language uses English-like statements (1) so it is easy for humans to read and write (1)'.
**State/Give** (1 mark): a short fact, e.g. 'Assembly language' or 'Python'. No explanation needed.
**Explain** (2-3 marks): make a point, then say WHY, using 'because' or 'so that'. Example: 'Machine code is processor dependent (1) because each CPU type has its own instruction set (1)'.
**Compare** (3-4 marks): give a feature and both sides: 'High-level is portable whereas low-level is specific to one processor type'. Each pair of statements gains the mark.
**Discuss** (6 marks): both sides, linked to the scenario, with a final justified conclusion. Aim for 3-4 developed points; do not just list definitions.
Always use the **key terms**: translator, mnemonic, portable, machine code, binary, hardware, one-to-many, memory efficient.
For 'why would a programmer use a low-level language' say specifically: direct control of hardware, smaller and faster programs, suitable for embedded systems with limited memory.
For 'why use a high-level language' say: easier to read and write, quicker to develop, easier to debug, portable between computers.
Do not just write 'it is faster' or 'it is easier': say faster to execute or to write, and why.
Examples score only with an explanation; name Python or Java as high-level and assembly/machine code as low-level.
Check the command word and mark count: the number of marks tells you how many distinct points you need.

mistakes.r: Low-level means close to the hardware, not simple. They are harder to read and write; high-level languages are easier for humans.
mistakes.w: Low-level languages are easier to use because they are 'low'.

mistakes.r: Machine code needs no translator; an assembler translates assembly language into machine code.
mistakes.w: Machine code is translated by an assembler.

mistakes.r: They are usually less efficient, but they are quicker to write, easier to debug and portable; for most applications the difference in speed does not matter.
mistakes.w: High-level languages are always slower and bad.

mistakes.r: Assembly uses mnemonics and has to be assembled; machine code is pure binary. Each assembly instruction maps to one machine code instruction.
mistakes.w: Assembly language is the same as machine code.

mistakes.r: The CPU only understands machine code, so high-level code must first be translated by a compiler or interpreter.
mistakes.w: A high-level language runs directly on the CPU.

mistakes.r: Portable means it can be used on different types of computer or processor with little or no change.
mistakes.w: Portable means the program is small.

mistakes.r: Low-level is only better where hardware control, speed or small memory are essential (embedded systems); it takes longer to develop and is not portable.
mistakes.w: Low-level is better for all programs because it is faster.

mistakes.r: One high-level statement usually becomes many machine code instructions; the one-to-one relationship applies to assembly.
mistakes.w: One high-level line becomes one machine code instruction.

summary: OCR J277 2.5.1 asks you to know the characteristics, purpose, advantages and disadvantages of high-level languages and low-level languages (assembly language and machine code), including why each is used and how they relate to translators. It matters because every programming question about languages, translators or embedded systems depends on understanding this trade-off between ease of use and hardware control.

terms.d: A programming language that uses English-like statements and is designed to be easy for humans to read and write; it needs translating into machine code before it can run.
A programming language that is close to the hardware and the CPU's instruction set; machine code and assembly language are the two types.
Instructions written in binary that the CPU can execute directly without translation.
A low-level language that uses mnemonics instead of binary; it is translated into machine code by an assembler.
A short abbreviated code, such as ADD or LDA, used in assembly language to represent a machine code instruction.
The program as written by the programmer in a high-level or assembly language, before it is translated.
The machine code produced when a translator converts source code.
Software that converts source code into machine code; the types are assembler, compiler and interpreter.
Able to be used on different types of computer or processor with little or no change.
Hiding unnecessary detail so a programmer can work with simpler ideas; high-level languages hide hardware details.
The part of a machine code instruction that says which operation to carry out.
The part of an instruction that gives the data, or the address of the data, to be used.
The complete set of machine code instructions that a particular type of processor can carry out.
A computer system built into a larger device to perform a dedicated function, often with limited memory and processing power.
A file of machine code that can be run directly by the computer without further translation.

worked.ans: High-level languages use English-like statements so they are easy for humans to read and write (1), whereas low-level languages use mnemonics or binary which are hard to read (1). High-level programs are portable and can run on different types of processor once translated (1), whereas low-level programs are written for one processor type and will not run on another (1).
worked.q: Describe two differences between a high-level language and a low-level language. [4]
steps: Pick two features: readability and portability (or translation).
Make a point for each language and show the contrast; each difference is worth 2 marks (one for each side or for the point and a reason).

worked.ans: A washing machine is an embedded system with limited memory, so the program must be small and efficient. A low-level language such as assembly lets the programmer control exactly which memory and registers are used, which produces compact code that runs quickly on the limited processor. The hardware inside the machine never changes, so the lack of portability of low-level code is not a problem. However, low-level programs take longer to write and are harder to debug and maintain, which increases cost. A high-level language would be quicker to develop and easier to update, but the translated code is usually larger and less efficient and might not fit in the available memory. Overall, a low-level language is more suitable because memory is limited and the hardware is fixed, although a high-level language could be considered if memory allowed.
worked.q: A company is writing the control program for a washing machine with a very small amount of memory. Discuss whether a high-level or low-level language should be used. [6]
steps: Identify scenario features: embedded system, very limited memory, fixed hardware, one purpose.
Advantages of low-level: compact, efficient code, direct control of hardware, hardware never changes so portability is not needed.
Disadvantages: slow and difficult to write, debug and maintain, needs expert programmers.
Advantages of high-level: quicker and cheaper to develop, easier to test and update, but translated code may be larger and slower.

worked.ans: The CPU can only execute machine code, which is binary (1). Python is a high-level language written in English-like statements, so it is not in a form the processor understands (1). It must first be translated into machine code by an interpreter or compiler (1).
